prime.problem: A benchmark says your agent solves 97% of tasks, yet users hit failures constantly. Both can be true: one number counts a task as solved if any of k tries worked, while a user only ever gets one try, every time.
prime.fits: You met pass@3 and pass^3 as counts on a tasks × trials grid in the agent-evals card, and p<sup>N</sup> for chained steps in compounding errors. This card turns those into formulas, honest estimators from n trials, and a rule for which one to report.
expect: averaging per task, then over tasks
prime.goal: Compute pass@k and pass^k from a task's n trials and c passes without bias, and argue which one a given agent should be judged on.

attend: Why does adding trials push pass@k up and pass^k down from the same per-trial p?
What does counting k-subsets of n trials buy you over just raising c/n to the k-th power?
Why does τ-bench compute pass^k per task and then average, instead of using one overall p?
In which setups is pass@k the honest number, and what makes pass^k the honest one for a customer-facing agent?
What happens to the pass^k estimate when trials are less independent than real users would be?

must: k independent trials with per-trial chance p → all pass with p<sup>k</sup>, at least one with 1 − (1 − p)<sup>k</sup> → as k grows one heads to 0 and the other to 1 → a 70% agent reads 97% at pass@3 and 34% at pass^3
A user gets one run each time, with no picker choosing the best of k → their experience over k visits is all-k-succeed → pass^k, not pass@k, measures reliability for agents that act for people

Raising a noisy c/n to the k-th power inflates it on average → the plug-in (c/n)<sup>k</sup> overstates reliability (0.397 vs a true 0.343 at p=0.7, n=8, k=3) → count all-pass k-subsets instead: C(c,k) ÷ C(n,k) is exactly unbiased

Failures cluster on hard tasks → per-task rates vary at the same overall average → p<sup>k</sup> of the average badly underestimates mean per-task pass^k (0.058 vs 0.500) → estimate per task, then average across tasks
elevated: The estimators need n ≥ k trials per task, and pass^k is exactly 0 whenever c < k → large k costs many trials per task, and small c can't distinguish 'rarely all pass' from 'never'
reference: Chen et al. (2021) introduced the unbiased pass@k estimator 1 − C(n−c,k) ÷ C(n,k)
τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024) introduced pass^k, read "pass hat k"
Python's math.comb(n, k) computes n choose k
Wolfe's example: o4-mini at 26% pass^4 on τ²-bench Telecom
avg@k: mean success over k trials, an estimate of p

compress.prompt: Card closed: in 3–5 sentences, explain why pass@k and pass^k move in opposite directions with k, how to estimate pass^k from n trials without bias, and which one you would report for a support agent. Or draw the chain from 'p per trial' to 'what a repeat user experiences'.
checklist: pass@k = 1 − (1 − p)<sup>k</sup> rises, pass^k = p<sup>k</sup> falls; equal at k = 1
users get every run, so pass^k matches their experience; pass@k fits when a verifier picks the best of k
estimate pass^k per task as C(c,k) ÷ C(n,k), not (c/n)<sup>k</sup>, which is biased upward
average per-task values across tasks, because failures cluster
assumes independent trials and a correct grader; needs n ≥ k

retrieve.q: A colleague says "pass@8 is 99.99%, so the agent is basically perfect." Explain what that number does and doesn't tell you, using p = 0.7.
answer: at p = 0.7, pass@8 = 1 − 0.3<sup>8</sup> ≈ 99.99%: almost any task gets solved once in 8 tries
the same agent has pass^8 = 0.7<sup>8</sup> = 5.8%: 8 runs in a row nearly never all succeed
a user who gets one run each visit lives with pass^k

retrieve.q: Walk through estimating pass^3 and pass@3 for the Tuesday task with n = 8 trials and c = 5 passes.
answer: C(8,3) = 56 possible groups of 3 trials
all-pass groups: C(5,3) = 10 → pass^3 = 10 ÷ 56 = 0.179
all-fail groups: C(3,3) = 1 → pass@3 = 1 − 1 ÷ 56 = 0.982
the plug-in (5/8)<sup>3</sup> = 0.244 would overstate pass^3

retrieve.q: You have budget for 400 runs. Do you run 50 tasks × 8 trials to report pass^8, or 100 tasks × 4 trials to report pass^4? What does each choice cost you?
answer: pass^k needs n ≥ k per task, so pass^8 forces at least 8 trials per task
more tasks shrink the task-to-task uncertainty, which usually dominates
pass^4 on 100 tasks is better measured; pass^8 tells you about longer streaks but on fewer tasks
state k either way; the numbers aren't comparable across k

retrieve.q: Two agents both pass 70% of all trials. Why can one have pass^8 of 0.058 and the other 0.500, and which estimator design captures that?
answer: one fails evenly (every task 0.7), the other clusters failures on hard tasks (1.0, 1.0, 0.4, 0.4)
mean of per-task p<sup>8</sup> differs even though the mean p is the same
τ-bench computes pass^k per task and averages, which keeps the clustering

compare.q: The agent-evals card reported pass^3 as a count on a 10 × 3 grid (4 of 10 tasks). How does C(c,k) ÷ C(n,k) generalise that count, and when do the two give the same answer?
answer: with n = k = 3, C(c,3) ÷ C(3,3) is 1 if c = 3 else 0: exactly the 'all 3 passed' count
with n > k it averages over every group of k trials, using all n runs
both are per task, then averaged across tasks
neither comes with an interval; that is the error-bars card's job

compare.q: Compounding errors multiplies per-step success over N steps; pass^k multiplies per-trial success over k runs. What is the same, what differs, and how does each fail as a prediction?
answer: same arithmetic: everything must go right, so chances multiply (0.95<sup>10</sup> ≈ 60%)
p<sup>N</sup> chains steps inside one task; pass^k repeats the whole task
both assume independence; clustered failures make measured pass^k sit far above p<sup>k</sup> (τ-bench retail: below 25% measured vs 2% predicted)
checking each step changes p<sup>N</sup>; nothing inside one run changes how many users hit a bad run

predict.q: A model upgrade lifts every task's per-trial success from 0.70 to 0.80. Before computing: does pass^8 go up by about 14%, about 2×, or about 3×? And pass@8?
predict.answer: pass^8 goes from 0.7<sup>8</sup> = 0.058 to 0.8<sup>8</sup> = 0.168, about 2.9×. pass@8 barely moves: 99.993% to 99.9997%. Small gains in p are amplified by the k-th power in pass^k and invisible in pass@k, which is why reliability work shows up in pass^k and not in pass@k.

apply.task: By hand, then with code/pass-k.py: a task ran n = 10 times with c = 7 passes. Compute pass^3, pass@3 and the plug-in (c/n)3. Then change one line so the script prints all three for your own agent's per-task counts and averages them across tasks.
apply.done: You get pass^3 = 35 ÷ 120 = 0.292, pass@3 = 1 − 1 ÷ 120 = 0.992 and plug-in 0.343, and your script prints a per-task table plus the across-task means.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the size of the pass^8 jump, or how little pass@8 moved?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the plug-in is biased, or why per-task averaging matters?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: per-trial p → pass^k, or clustered failures → pass^k above p<sup>k</sup>?
For your own agent, which number would you report, and what k matches how often a user hits the same task?
What would make your trials less independent than real users, and how would that bias your pass^k?
